wrong: Buildings with no CAT1 test filed for the current year.
right: Buildings that skipped a whole annual cycle.
why: In August the year is not over, so "has not filed yet" is the calendar rather than a lapse. Five buildings in six on that list were simply not due.

wrong: Buildings the shortlist had not sampled before, counted as new.
right: Buildings with something the city itself published inside the window.
why: Not one of the 457 had a city-dated event in the window and their violations were a median of 32 days old. The count was measuring our own sampling, which rotates 2,200 buildings out of 12,323 on every run.

wrong: A blocklist of 35 directory brands; anything unmatched was published.
right: Positive evidence only: a government record, or a host tied to the firm.
why: 967 of the 1,211 published for no better reason than failing to match a brand name, and cityrealty, nybits, local.yahoo, nextdoor and a rentmanager tenant portal all passed. A blocklist puts every directory nobody has thought of on the allow side.

wrong: Detect likely private individuals and drop those cards.
right: Print a name only where something vouches that it is a business; keep the card and identify it by address otherwise.
unit: per cent of cards keeping a name
why: Detection topped out at 84% recall, so roughly one private individual in six still reached the register — and the ones that got through were the names no public file happened to hold.
